utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brdjanin. As usual, I would like to know whether you can hear me in a language that you can understand. THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour, yes, I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good morning, to you. I put the same question, can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, general, you may sit down. Appearances? For the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, Anna Richterova and Denise Gustin, case manager for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, to you. Mr. Ackerman, sorry appearance for Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman, along with my co-counsel Milka Maglov and legal assistant Tania Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for General Talic. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] I'm Xavier de Roux and I'm assisted by Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, and I hope we will see you more often, Maitre de Roux. How are you feeling? Are you better? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] [In English] I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any way, I suggest at some point in time you try to have a word with your client. The Chamber has kept itself informed on your application to have Madam Fauveau appointed as co-counsel and the decision of the Registry was communicated to your client during yesterday's sitting. I suppose you are aware of it, but I think that a short talk, tete-a-tete with your client at this point in time is in order. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] I will speak with my client in a minute after the pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Most kind, Maitre de Roux. So are there any preliminaries this morning?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, not a preliminary but at the end of the sitting I would like to raise what happened yesterday in the Stakic trial because Defence counsel aren't aware in terms of -- I think Mr. Ackerman saw some or heard some of the hearing, but it does affect this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't had a chance to consult Judge Schomburg as yet. I'll be meeting Judge Schomburg on something completely different but I suppose --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's really to put Defence counsel in the picture on the record, as it were. Defence counsel in this case, because that's the trouble. Although what happened yesterday has an affect on this case, neither Defence counsel was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Okay. I thank you, Ms. Korner. Pleasures yet to come.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to erase the stain on my reputation and hand over the missing maps which we exhibited yesterday but without physical presence of the maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Actually, Mr. Ackerman was very sympathetic. Yes. Thank you. Please bring in the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, to you, Mr. Smailagic. You will be asked once more to make the solemn declaration that you made yesterday. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Madam Richterova for the Prosecution will continue with her examination, direct examination of you and pleas may I remind you to answer just the question and nothing but the question, and Ms. Richterova to pause a little while after he's finished giving his statement. So that the translators will have enough time to complete their interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Smailagic. I would like --

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like you to remind what we were talking about right before the session was adjourned. You mentioned that the main parties in Banja Luka held interparty meetings and that at the beginning, during these interparty meetings, there were attempts at reaching agreements. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you said that there -- at the beginning, it means did the situation change later?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Which way did the relationship between parties change?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the system of communication weakened and that happened when the war commenced in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And how would you describe the relationship between parties after the war started and when the relationship deteriorated?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war in Croatia, a mobilisation was proclaimed of the population, the population in Banja Luka was mobilised. We were against this mobilisation, that is to say the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the head, Mr. Izetbegovic, called for there not to be a response to the mobilisation. And on one occasion, that was the main subject at one of the meetings for mobilisation and since then, the relations deteriorated. We tried to persuade people not to respond to the mobilisation, to persuade our population not to respond to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Why was that? I mean that you tried to persuade people not to answer the mobilisation order?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was not a war. We hadn't been attacked as a state. We felt that we were morally justified in not -- we felt we didn't have the moral right to influence and to participate in the war which had commenced in Croatia. We thought it was unjust.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what were the comments of other parties of -- or one party, whoever made comments regarding these mobilisations?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time the HDZ stopped communicating, probably because for reasons known to them, and only the SDS called some of our representatives to meetings on several occasions and tried to persuade us. However, these meetings always turned into very, very unpleasant situations. There were -- insults were even hurled and threats were made.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you were talking about insults and threats, can you assist the judges and briefly state some threats or some statements which you felt as threats?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning, it started by belittling and humiliating our president, Mr. Izetbegovic and then it boiled down to making threats issuing threats to us. If we didn't respond to the mobilisation, we would have to leave Banja Luka ourselves. Even then, the Republika Srpska had unofficially been proclaimed and at a public appearance, and we reacted to this, as a party, with the SDS party, if I can mention this person, Mr. Brdjanin, Mr. Vukic said at a meeting sometime in the summer of 1991, they said that the army was Serbian and that not a single bullet from the barracks wouldn't be taken out. And that the army was now theirs. At that point, we felt that the situation had deteriorated quite a bit and later, the meetings were very rare. There were almost no meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In case you said there were almost no meetings, were there some official or unofficial contacts between SDA and SDS and if yes, what was discussed during these contacts?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The official meetings had stopped but there were some unofficial ones since we had an office next to them. Sometimes they would call us, come and have a look at something, come and discuss something, sometimes we even insisted on a meeting because there were threats and disorder at sessions of the at the assembly, the Municipal Assembly because we had our delegates there. The objective of these talks was to see how we could help the population in Banja Luka because the population was afraid, a mobilisation had been proclaimed and we attempted to do something here, but there were no results.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us during these meetings or conversation, were there any subjects or proposals made by members of SDS in which they could express their nationalistic views?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. At one meeting, an unofficial meeting, when we energetically rejected their proposals, Mr. Brdjanin said literally, "Well, aren't you ashamed? You're walking around on Serbian territory, it's all Serbian." That was quite a significant warning to ourselves with regard to the situation, what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you mentioned Mr. Brdjanin, did Mr. Brdjanin attend these interparty meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was there on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you -- did he express some other views? Did he held some speeches during these interparty meetings or unofficial meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nothing in general, but as I understand it, Mr. Brdjanin, we sometimes thought that he was joking. He made some very serious threats but there were most quarrels among the members of the SDS, that is to say their executive board.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you stop you now? When you, before, said that, I will quote, "Mr. Brdjanin said literally, "Well aren't you ashamed? You are walking around on Serbian territory. It is all Serbian," did he explain why he was saying this was Serbian territory? Did he make any comment, further comment?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He made comments which you might call comments. They weren't really so. Since we were used to his provocations, to these provocation that is they directed at us. That this was this had been Serbian territory for centuries, that we had been converted to the Turkish system and that we had taken their territory, he would say things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you use -- did he use some names when he was referring to non-Serb people?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean names of individuals or in general?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I mean general, in general.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, well, he tried to use words to provoke us in order to insult us as much as possible. He very often and especially in some of his public appearances he very often used the word "balija." I doubt that he knew what balija, the word "balija" meant, but in fact for an ordinary man, an uneducated man, someone who has no culture, so that's what mean -- that's what the word would mean, so it could relate to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Excuse me, what does this expression "balija" mean?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Balija, in fact, means a man who is not educated, who behaves badly, rude, someone who is rude, in short, an impolite man, a simple man.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I would like to return to these meetings between parties. Were -- who else apart of Mr. Brdjanin, who else was present?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me a moment, Your Honour, I may have missed it, but I don't think it's been established when these meetings were taking place. I believe they were prior to the time of the indictment but I think it should be established when they were so that the Trial Chamber would be able to evaluate them better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think your observation is perfectly in order and perhaps Ms. Richterova, you could put the question direct to your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, are you able to tell us when these meetings took place?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the multi-party elections, the formation of the government, I'm thinking of the municipal authorities in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, no. I mean when we were discussing now the meetings or informal meetings when Mr. Brdjanin started expressing his attitude, when these meetings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The period of time, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Of course I do not want to hear exact day because I believe you do not remember it. It's ten years ago but --

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these meetings, roughly speaking, started to be held around the middle or the beginning of the summer, June or July, when the war in Croatia had been going on for two or three months already. That's when it started, and I think it happened after the mobilisation. That mobilisation was in May or June in Banja Luka, in 1991. So the middle of 1991 is when these meetings started, and they didn't last for long. Towards the end of the year, they stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you are talking about the mobilisation for the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: That's the answer, Mr. Ackerman. Can I go now and I would repeat my last question and it was, who else was present during these meetings? And I would like you to talk about meetings which took place towards the end of 1991 or 1992, if there were some meetings.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at these meetings almost the entire executive committee attended them. Mr. Vukic was there, the president of the SDS in Banja Luka. Mr. Brdjanin. Mr. Kupresanin. On several occasions, Mr. Zupljanin was present and there were --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you assist us and again tell us which speeches struck your attention, which you felt as threatening or which you felt uneasy with them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I think this exact question has been previously asked and answered. Almost in exactly the same words.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, but this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. Let me interject. No. There is a slight difference, Mr. Ackerman, without the need of actually asking Ms. Richterova to comment on your objection. Because the previous question has been directed to establish who else, apart from your client, used to be present at these meetings. Now, this question that is being asked now is obviously directed to establish whether there were other statements made by anyone of these persons present that may have attracted witness's attention more than others. So for the time being, for whatever it is worth, I will accept the question and direct the witness to answer it. He has also heard what I had to say and perhaps it is more clear to him what is expected from him. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I have checked the transcript, Your Honour, and you're correct her previous question was about things that Mr. Brdjanin had said and that has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As far as Mr. Brdjanin is concerned, yes, but now the question is a sequence -- a sequence to the previous one which referred to who else used to be present at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if there were any other statements made during these meetings, don't forget that we have here the charge of joint criminal enterprise and this and that, so this is why I'm allowing the question for whatever it is worth. Because obviously, I mean one has to give it weight later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that she's now asking people other than Brdjanin and I had not understood that she had not asked that question before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Smailagic, please, you've heard the question. You are being asked to state whether -- of the statements that you may have heard in the course of these meetings at which you mentioned these persons as being present, which statements attracted your attention. If there were any. You have already stated that there were some made by Mr. Brdjanin. Were there any other statements that attracted your attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There were. They would take the floor, all of them, and speak. However, what attracted my attention, not only my attention but the attention of others, were the statements given by Mr. Vukic, the president of the SDS. He also used the same threatening expressions, and he would always first attack Mr. Izetbegovic and then continued by saying that we should give up his policy if we wanted to remain with the rest of the population in Banja Luka. So those were the threats that he made in this indirect manner. There were others as well, but more subdued.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, I will ask you slightly different question. Is there any difference between Muslim and Serbian first name or surname?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a difference between Muslim and Serbian names. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was that ever a topic that was raised during these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The topic was raised on a number of occasions. Now, I can recall for instance that there was talk about our allegedly -- alleged Serbian origin, that we should all be Serbs actually. To put it simply, that we should change our names.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did it happen?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such cases in Banja Luka, a significant number of people did change their names. Some out of fear, some because of the threats. What is interesting is the fact that in most of the cases, the individuals were women. They took Serb names.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you personally talk to anybody who would change his name?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I even had a neighbour who changed his name. His name was Omer and he changed it to Jovan. May I explain?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Excuse me, and did he state the reason?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I once went to his home on private business, his wife opened the door and I asked whether Omer was there, and she said, "There is no Omer here. He's Jovan now." But he was not at home. Later, I met him in the street. He had already been mobilised and was wearing a uniform. He was a member of the military and I said, "Is it true that you've changed your name?" And he said, "Yes. It made me feel safer." But although he didn't say, most probably he did it under pressure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will change the subject and I will go from interparty meetings into any public -- public meetings, in 1991, 1992, were there any political rallies in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were. Especially from late May until early autumn. SDS organised such rallies very frequently because of the war, and it was during one of these rallies, I believe that it happened in May or June, maybe even July, that the loudest person was Mr. Brdjanin. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usually I give him permission.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What happened was that in Banja Luka, there was a joint movement which was actually not a party. It involved a number of citizens from different ethnic backgrounds and they organised a peaceful rally against the war in Croatia and they made statements in respect of everything that was going on. However, very soon the police dispersed the crowd and soon after that, a public rally was organised by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you remember who was present at that public rally who was organised by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually all of the members would be present at the -- at public rallies, but when the war started, we began seeing individuals in uniform on the stage. And in those speeches, and those addresses, the loudest person, as I said, was Mr. Brdjanin, with his threats, addressed to the Muslim and Croat population. There is a number of statements that he made during those rallies and not only during the rallies but also in various TV and radio programmes and also in the media, in the print, where he used very abusive language when speaking about Croats or Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will stop you now. And let's go step by step. When you said you saw Mr. Brdjanin at these rallies. Let's focus at rallies, at this particular one which you have in your mind or in case there were some others. What do you remember that was said by Mr. Brdjanin during these rallies? You said he was the loudest person. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are now to describing as these rallies generically. I think we need to be more specific, if we can, as to when the rally that he is speaking about occurred, as close as he can get rather than generically, a plural, bunch of rallies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Generically you are also right, Mr. Ackerman. Let me try and direct the witness myself for a while, if you don't mind, Ms. Richterova, and we will come to your question in any case. Mr. Smailagic, you used the word "rallies" in the plural. How many of these rallies are you aware of? Let's start from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were several such rallies. I am referring to the period of time starting in late May until winter; that is, during the time where people could be outside. There were least six or seven such rallies, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And to the best of your recollection again, in these rallies, as far as you can remember, was Mr. Brdjanin always present? And did he always speak? Or make a speech?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember whether he attended all of those rallies because his presence can only be remembered for the statements he made. Those statements were very detrimental for us, very intimidating, and instilled fear, not only amongst the Muslim population but amongst the Croats as well. Let me quote one of his first statements, which made us feel quite uneasy. One of such statements was, that is, one such statement that frightened us a lot, was that, "It was a sin and shame of every Serb to drink the same water as balijas." We knew, as early as that, that horrible things would happened and they did indeed happen subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Maitre de Roux? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm sorry to intervene, but I am somehow lost in the chronology. Are we talking about 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I figure it out from what I have been following on the monitor and also listening to the interpretation, we are talking of the end of 1991, as I gather it. That's because this is more or less happening at the same time the mobilisation started or immediately after. But you are right, Ms. Richterova, if you could perhaps be more specific in your question, in your questions, and if you could be more specific in your answers, you would narrow the gap, because as you understand, the objection or the remark, more than an objection, that was raised by Mr. Ackerman is very valid. You have every right to speak and tell us what you know about what Mr. Brdjanin said in these rallies but we -- Mr. Ackerman has also got the right to know how many of these rallies you're talking about, whether you were all -- you were present at all of these rallies or at only some of these rallies, whether Mr. Brdjanin spoke in all of these rallies, and if he spoke in some of these rallies, when were these rallies actually held. I can't help you more than that, and I will now leave you again in the hands of Ms. Richterova but please try to be as precise as possible in your answers. Thank you. I know it's not easy because you are a politician too, and therefore, you must have taken part in a large number of events and we are talking of events that happened ten years plus ago, but please try to concentrate as much as you can. No one is after your blood here. We are just trying to find out what happened, what happened in the course of these rallies that you are being questioned about. So Ms. Richterova, please. If you may either rephrase your question or put the question again to the witness, the witness now has more or less been briefed as to what is required from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to do my best and I will rephrase my questions. In fact, I will use some questions which you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you present at all of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Rallies actually because we are talking rallies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Excuse me, rallies.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the time that has gone by and all of the events, I cannot remember exactly how many rallies I attended. But I'm sure that I attended most of them, because I was curious, of course. In view of the situation it concerned us, and it was my moral obligation to be present at such rallies. I felt it that way. One of such statements, apart from the one that I have already quoted, was even more frightening. Though I'm unable to tell you the exact date, when it was said, again, from the end of May until beginning of September, roughly, but I'm -- I would like to stress that I do remember these statements very well. I have already quoted one of them, there was another one something to the effect that we had no business to do on sacred Serbian land. Then another one, which was uttered at -- during an autumn rally. It is a custom in our country to buy large quantities of cabbage in that period of -- in that time of the year, to make sauerkraut, and during one such rallies he said, and this was broadcast by the TV, "I should like to tell the balijas that they should not be buying cabbage because they will not have time to eat it." There was a number of such statements, all of them including very abusive, offensive language. There was another one, he said, "There is a proverb, a balija proverb which says, 'Whoever hits you with a stone, you should give him back a piece of bread.' Whereas us Serbs, our prover says, 'Whoever hits you with a stone, you should hit him back with two.'" All of these statements affected us considerably and we felt them really bad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richterova, perhaps you have noticed that witness has not told us who is making these statements and perhaps you could direct the question to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, I knew you were -- whom you were referring but we just missed this part. Who did make these speeches you were just quoting?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The speeches, the statements, were exclusively uttered by Mr. Brdjanin. I don't know whether he acted in any official capacity by doing so, but that is what he said. There were others who took part as well but never made such statements, never spoke in this manner. Those were his words. As for the thing that he said about the cabbage, he repeated it twice during one of the rallies and during a TV interview. He made quite a few interviews for the Banja Luka, the Serb TV, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, I would like to stop you and as we discuss it at the beginning, I will try to ask you questions and you will answer my question, if you could limit your answer to my questions. And I perfectly understand that you want to tell us everything, not to forget anything. But to follow the events, the chronology of events, it is easier for us if you will answer just my questions. We will return to these rallies. What effect did these speeches have on non-Serb population in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is no foundation for that question. It's not been established whether he knows what effect it had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you rephrase your question, then, Ms. Richterova, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What effect did these speeches have on you?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The speeches affected us frightfully. People were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question was, "What effect did it have on you?" He's answering the first question, what effect did it have on all the people. And I would insist that he answer the question that was asked and that is what effect it had on him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Smailagic, please, the question was directed as to your own personal reaction to these statements that you heard during these rallies. Answer that question first, and then if there are further questions directed to you, as to whether you know whether others were affected also by these statements, you would be able to answer that question as well. You don't need to put the question again. You have put it already. So how did these statements affect you, if they did, at all? You personally, as Mr. Smailagic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had a very frightening effect. We realised that the situation was very tense and I felt scared and other people felt scared as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you discuss these speeches with other people?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I must now kindly ask Mr. President to allow me to explain this in more detail. I had many friends amongst Serbs and Croats as well, but mostly amongst Serbs, because of the people that I socialised with. After such rallies, many of my Serb friends told me, "You should be careful. This doesn't augur well." And they criticised Mr. Brdjanin. I would not like to mention their names for reasons of their safety but what I'm trying to tell the Court is that there were quite a few Serbs, ordinary Serbs, who were saddened to hear his speeches. The fear had already reached its peak amongst the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will now move on other occasions, if there were some other occasions, where you see -- saw Brdjanin in person or if you saw him on TV, heard him on radio?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him on TV on a number of occasions. I watched TV in particular such programmes on a regular basis, that is the programmes which concerned the rallies which he attended. So I did see him on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you could ask him again to specify which period of time he's referring to, because this is important.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I was just going to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When was it that you saw him on TV? And I would like you also to tell us, if you recall any statements heard by Brdjanin on TV, to tell us approximately the period of time you heard it.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I described a moment ago took place in 1991, because it was during that period of time that most of such statements were made, though they continued in 1992. As for his TV appearances, I remember only the appearances when he made specific statements, but the TV would often report his statements and his speeches, all of which included threats expressed to the Bosniak population and non-Serb population in general. He often said, "Whoever is not with us is against us." So that was repeated quite often.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And a last question regarding these appearances on TV or radio, you said he -- he expressed threats against Bosnian population. To the best of your recollection, do you remember any particular speeches which you felt as a threat?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of such threats, for instance, was that we better go back to Turkey. He was actually quoting something that Mr. Vuk Draskovic had said on an earlier occasion. Then on another occasion, he repeated what he had already said, "That it was a sacred Serb land and that Muslims," that is balijas, as he referred to them, "had no right to walk on that land." So it was in that spirit, in that sense, that he made his statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did he ever said how many of Serbs should leave Banja Luka? He said -- of non-Serbs should leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he made that particular statement in 1992, early 1992. It was at the time when non-Serb population, but also a certain number of Serbs, had started leaving abroad. He said, "We would keep between 3 and 5 per cent of balijas here, to make them do humiliating jobs, the jobs which were humiliating for Serbs." I'm talking about 1992 now. At that time, Banja Luka had a street which was called Gospodska Ulica where people walked around in the evening and he said, "Those who remain will have to lick Serb shoes in Gospodska Ulica, Gospodska Street. " So this was just another example of the statements that he made and that affected us profoundly, affected myself and others as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you personally heard -- hear this speech on TV?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will now move further and I want to ask series of questions about the life in Banja Luka. What effect had the war in Croatia on the life of people in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, everything had been disturbed, disrupted, nothing was normal any more. Security was in non-existent, the security of non-Serbian citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, I would like you now to say, to only summarise various aspects which changed, just give me -- give the Judges the list of aspects which changed and then we will develop them.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most important change was the fact that circulation was limited, movement was limited. This was in 1992. In order to move freely, it was necessary to have a pass. Secondly, if you were a civilian, in civilian clothing, there was always the possibility of your papers being checked and a Bosniak or non-Serb could have very unpleasant experiences in such cases. There were beatings and maltreatment and the like. That's how it started and then they continued on to other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Maitre de Roux? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this testimony is difficult to follow because the question that was put to the witness concerns, if I have understood it well, the situation in Banja Luka during the war, with Croatia. That's what I can read here. However, the war with Croatia finished on the 3rd of January, 1992, and now the witness is speaking to us about security in 1992. So I don't think he's answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Maitre de Roux, I think I will let him answer the question as he likes and then we draw our conclusions afterwards. In reality, the question as put to him according to me, covers the whole period of the war in Croatia and certainly does not exclude also the aftermath of the war. If he can, of course, distinguish and be more precise, that would be more helpful to you and to the Trial Chamber. But as phrased, the question covers both the period of the war and the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. aftermath of the war. But if you can distinguish between the two, for example, I would imagine from what we have heard already, information with regard to mobilisation of troops inside of Banja Luka during the war in Croatia, after the war in Croatia, I'm sure it was not the same. I'm sure you are in a position to give us information on that. So please try to be more specific in giving your answer and try to answer the question that was put to you in the way it was put to you. For the time being, we just want a list, for example if there was shortage of food, I don't know, I mean -- I'm just thinking aloud about something that may have occurred or may not have occurred. If you just say there was shortage of food, troops, more troops on the territory of Banja Luka. Just give us a list. And then Ms. Richterova -- Dr. Richterova then can proceed with asking you for more details later. Yes, Mr. Smailagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were just speaking about 1991, when the war in Croatia was being waged. Banja Luka did not have a lot of food [As interpreted]. The events that happened in Croatia, such events happened in Slovenia first of all. The Yugoslav army was there at that point. All the forces from Slovenia too and then when the war in Croatia finished --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you're not interested in Slovenia, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, that's not it. I understand what the witness said was "Banja Luka was not out of food" and the translation says, "Banja Luka did not have a lot of food."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard. That's what I heard him say, or at least not him say it, the translation. "There wasn't a lot of food." That's what was translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that's not what he said. What he said was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know what he said in B/C/S, definitely not. And my congratulations to you if you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have a couple of people here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can ask him to -- yes, there seems to be some sort of an either wrong interpretation, translation of what you said or we need to clarify it any way. When you referred to the -- to food in Banja Luka, during the conflict in Croatia, did you say that there was ample food, there was sufficient food, or that there was not sufficient food during the war in Croatia? In Banja Luka, obviously.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that there was enough food and that was no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you were right, Mr. Ackerman, the translation was not correct. Thank you. You can proceed now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, I would like to rephrase my question because we have on previous occasion heard about the war in Croatia. Now I would like to ask you specifically about Banja Luka from April, 1992, until the end of April. How at that time the life for non-Serbs change? And as I said at the beginning, please give me a list and we will go back to each of these topics separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question I know wasn't intended but Ms. Richterova said from April until the end of April. I think she means something different otherwise the witness would be fairly restricted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The end of the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: 1992 to the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I would suggest to you until or unless I stop you, that to put direct questions to him. I mean, if you are going to -- if you want to know what was, for example, the security situation, if you want to know, what was the food situation, if you want to know what was the electricity supply situation, go direct. I will allow you to do that until there may come a point at which I may need to stop you. But in the meantime, I think we will get where you want to get where we all want to get, quicker. So please proceed with putting a direct question one after the other. And then if you want to add further questions after that, of course, to get more detail, of course, you will be allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It will be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You already mentioned the restriction of movement. In which way this restriction -- in which way the movement was restricted?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to ask for a -- for permission to explain my answer to this question, because at the end of the year of 1991, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a referendum had been announced for the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina from Yugoslavia and for it to be recognised as an independent state and since that date, a lot of pressure was already being exerted on all of us. Pressure was brought to bear as far as the SDS party is concerned, in order to prevent this referendum from being held. Now I'm going to turn to 1992, towards the end of February or March, I really can't remember exactly, a referendum was held in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Banja Luka. The referendum was organised and held in very difficult circumstances. As we had -- I apologise, Mr. President, but I really have to explain this, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A question was -- I tried to intervene myself. The idea being to try to streamline the series of questions simplify the whole process, of course you are referring -- this is not April, 1992. But do you have any comments, Maitre de Roux? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the question concerned the restriction of movement in Banja Luka and we are now speaking about the referendum and independence. To be frank, I don't understand anything any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They may be related and in fact what we heard in previous sittings they are definitely related, but I suppose he can answer the question. The question was very direct, starting from April 1992 onwards until the end of the year, what do you have to state, to tell us, with regard to restriction of one's personal movement? So go ahead. If you think this restriction was the result of the holding of the referendum two months before, just state it, but you don't need to explain. I mean we have been told the whole story already by persons who are qualified to give us the picture of -- the historical survey of the events that took place at the time. So please try to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was one of the reasons -- the referendum was one of the reasons for having a reign of terror in Banja Luka, introducing such a reign. In May 1992, they had already started with work obligations, mobilising people for work obligations, and whoever responded to this mobilisation, for work obligations, or reported to military units, would receive a pass which would allow him to move freely. And only such people were able to move freely through the town. If anyone didn't have a pass he would be arrested, maltreated and sent off to do work obligations. Not only people who were fit for work were sent to do work obligations, but all people who were of non-Serbian nationality were sent to do such work. I have to give you an example which concerns myself. I've been a disabled pensioner since 1986. I had a decision from the disability commission, and I was called up to do -- to carry out my work obligation. When I received the first call-up, I sent my wife. And in the middle of the day, they would start beating in the street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have to stop you, Mr. Smailagic. The question is restricted only for the time being on movement restrictions, restrictions of movement. So please try to answer that. You will definitely be asked questions on what happened in other fields of life, to you personally and to others that you are aware of. But for the time being, because the way you are handling the examination-in-chief is disruptive also to the Prosecution, in the sense that -- I have to stop you because otherwise you will get us all lost completely. I mean, when Maitre de Roux says that he can not follow, I appreciate what he is saying. It's difficult even for us to follow. So please try to answer that question. There were restrictions on one's movement. And you explained also that those who accepted the mobilisation rules and reported to work and to barracks, et cetera, were given a pass. Do you have anything else to add with regard to restrictions of movements, starting April, 1992, ending December 1992? And if the situation changed, got better, worse, or stopped, during these months, please tell us -- give us the details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They had introduced a curfew too. So there was a curfew and movement was restricted. So the situation from April until the end of the year got worse with every day. And I have to say the men moved around town very little. Mostly women went out and bought things and so on, for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, were you aware of establishment of checkpoints in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The roads in Banja Luka, some of the checkpoints there were -- the first ones were put I think on the 13th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was the purpose of these checkpoints, do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These checkpoints were set up only after the events in Sarajevo on the 12th of May, I think, give or take a day. These checkpoints served to check people, to check their papers, but they were used for other purposes. The regular police did not man these checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who manned these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were men who were dressed in uniforms. They had SOS, the SOS mark on their caps. They were well-known Banja Luka criminals. They were Serbs and Bosniaks and there were Croats too. They were mostly composed of well-known Banja Luka criminals, and when they would check people's papers. If they saw that the citizen whose papers they were checking had money in their wallet, they would take it immediately, or if they would see a ring on someone's hand, they would take it. So that was the purpose. They wanted to spread panic and unease among the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When did they appeared in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was after these disturbances in Sarajevo, around the 13th of May. That's the first time that I saw and heard from others, from my friends, about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you personally had any dealings with these SOS?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not personally because the part of the town in which I lived, we could say it's closer to the centre. There was not a checkpoint in that part of town, no barricades. But I had the opportunity to hear from my friends, from my colleagues, and some of them at the time were still employed then. I'm talking about -- I'm thinking about employed women. They would say, "We have been sent back from the checkpoint." At that time, some work was being done, but it was mostly women who were doing the work, who were employed. The men had work allegations or they had to do their military service. And when papers were being checked in the morning at the checkpoint, if they established that the woman was a Bosniak, they would send her back, they wouldn't let her pass through.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I probably missed, even though I followed the LiveNote, who were the -- did you said -- did you say how these criminals called themselves?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- on their caps they had a sign, SOS, the Serbian Armed Forces, which in fact means the Serbian Liberation Forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned the wrong doings of these people. Did the police do anything about these criminals?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did know. At one of these checkpoints, one of these checkpoints had been set up near the Mejdan Police Station and yes, they knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we use the map and if the witness could show us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The same map that you made use of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, only to assist the Judges, can you show where the Mejdan is, in which part of the town?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mejdan is on this stretch, it's down the Vrbas, but I can't see here because the letters are very small but it's somewhere here. Mejdan is at the very beginning of this path which is leading here. It's the continuation of this, because this is a neighbourhood which is fairly large and it is called Mejdan and the police station was here and a little below, maybe 50 metres below, there was a bridge which connected part of the town, called Carcepsi [phoen] with Burak [phoen]. And this is a path that people had to use when they were going to work. The checkpoint was here. So about 100 metres from the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, could you mark it with a pen, please? And put your initials next to it? Actually, yesterday, you showed us Mejdan. You had put a cross. If you look at where you were pointing just now and where you have marked, and go to about eight o-clock to the left, you will see Mejdan and you marked it for us yesterday. It's above Kotor Varos right in the last square --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: He got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, he got it, but it is important for us to know exactly where this checkpoint that you are referring to was. So please mark it on the map and put your initials next to it. You see the Banja Luka/Kotor Varos road.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's here. Mejdan and it's somewhere here, just allow me a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think Mr. Smailagic should use his glasses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's no use lending him mine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, it's in this street, the Danka Mitrova Street. In this street, the police station was in this street. And right here, in the vicinity, there is the bridge which goes over the Vrbas. It's here. But I don't have it marked here. This is the old bridge, the Rebrovac, but here, somewhere in the middle of this path, between this mark, the Rebrovac, or perhaps this mark that has been placed on the map here. So along the street Danka Mitrova there was the bridge, so I've just seen it. Here it is. This is the bridge. And there was a checkpoint on the bridge. And right here, in the vicinity, there was the police station. This bridge was the Studentski Most. That's what it was called. They knew about this barricade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think that's enough. Thank you. I would like to move on with another question. So we were talking about restriction of movement, about establishment of checkpoints. Are you aware of people who would lost their jobs during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a mass phenomenon. People would lose their jobs, especially if a member of the a family, a male member, failed to respond to the mobilisation call, the call-up to do a military service or to do work obligations or if his mother or sister had been removed from their -- dismissed from work. Sometime in May or June ... [no interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Glas newspaper which was published in Banja Luka, the name of which was later changed into Srpski Glas.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In this connection, I would like you to show a document which was premarked P254, and it is already part of Banja Luka collection. However, we have copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, they were supposed to give us a list of documents they were going to use with the witness. They didn't give us any list and this was certainly not provided to us in advance. We don't have all the documents here. Because there are thousands of them and I think we were told that the only documents that were going to be used were those which were attached to his witness statement, and so this comes as kind of a surprise to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not just to you, Mr. Ackerman, but also to us. Do I understand it, Ms. Richterova, that you will be, in the course of the next hour and a half after the break, making use of a number of documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I am going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or is it just this document for the moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: A part of this document. I am going to use right at the end of my appearance, three more documents, which were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Distributed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Which were disclosed and I can distribute them right now and we -- they weren't part of Banja Luka but they were disclosed under different witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but the thing is, the Defence have a right to know which -- this is a document that you are going to show now, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. I am going to show this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you inform the Defence which documents the witness was going to be asked to make reference to?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I would make -- I suggest we make use of the break now and you sort this out. It's a very simple problem. And perhaps you could also put us in a position where we know beforehand which documents we need to have before us. I do have a bundle which was given to us yesterday, but again, I don't know which documents you're referring to because these have a reference number 2.3 to 395 and they are not marked otherwise as -- oh, exhibit, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, these documents are translations. In fact, I asked yesterday whether you want all the exhibits and we were told no, that they can be distributed during the tendering of these -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we need to know beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: But I can -- we have enough copies so we can distribute them right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And this document exhibit number is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not among the ones that were given to us yesterday, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must complain rather loudly because we had an agreement that they weren't going to supply us copies of the exhibits, they were going to use, because that would be too burdensome but they would give us the list in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I had had this last night, it may have affected my preparation for cross-examination and that was the reason they were going to supply us in advance. We either give them copies or we tell in advance any documents we are going to use. That was the agreement, and this is not fair and I shouldn't now be expected to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right, Mr. Ackerman. I don't think you need to convert the converted. Ms. Korner, will you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's entirely my fault. I apologise. Ms. Richterova, of course, hasn't been in court. I forgot to tell her the system. We will sort it out and I'm sorry that Mr. Ackerman has been put in this position and Your Honours likewise, but it's not Ms. Richterova's fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. So please do take it in hand and we will reconvene at just before 11.00, 5 to 11.00. In the meantime I suppose this will be sorted out. You are right, Mr. Ackerman, you've got the Chamber's support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Would you bring in the witness, please? Yes, Ms. Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to ask one more question, in fact, I will repeat my question, which wasn't thoroughly answered because Mr. Smailagic was pointing at the map, the place where the checkpoints were established, that it was close to the police station, but he didn't answer the question whether police ever did anything against these people who manned these checkpoints. And to whom he was referring as criminals.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police never did anything in order to remove the checkpoints. However, they were eventually removed but I don't know when that was. As for the criminals, I was referring to individuals from Banja Luka who had been organised by someone and sent to the barricades. They were given weapons by them and they plundered people's property. Those were the criminals I was referring to. There were even cases of internal fights amongst them because of the spoils. A case of that kind occurred at one of the barricades here and I remember that a member of one of this SDS units was killed at one of the barricades by the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: That's enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Give a little bit of a pause because during the break, the interpreters explained to me the difficulties that they are passing through. So between his answer and your next question, allow at least a few seconds to go by.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I will return to document which we discussed before the adjournment, and I assume that now all parties and the Judges have the document. If I may ask you to show this document, which was marked a P254.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you see this document and did you read the article at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Richterova. This document consists of three pages, at least that's what we have here. You are obviously showing him the one which is a photo copy of, I suppose, the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The article itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to make ourselves understood, this is the document, Mr. Ackerman, this is the document that he is being obviously shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we do not have the document in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You must have because we placed them on your desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a three-page document starting with the first page being a translation into English of what is -- what appears in the document that the witness is now being shown. Yes, please go ahead, Mr. Smailagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you read this article at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am familiar with this document. It was a well-known decision signed by the president of the Crisis Staff of the Krajina, Mr. Brdjanin, and it concerned the restrictions in terms of employment of non-Serbs to the effect that all non-Serb leaders and managers should be removed from their positions. The decision was implemented. That is the employment was limited. I cannot read the words here, the print is too small for me, but I do remember the text itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I only want to point that as a part of the Banja Luka binder or collection is the exact decision which was issued, and on which based this article was issued. Did this decision had any effect on you personally?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. The document was just one more confirmation of what we believed could happen to us. I had a very large family and all members of my family lost their jobs. After this decision, the situation generally speaking was disrupted. I think that it was passed after the outbreak of conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It said that all who did not take part at the plebiscite were not considered as equal citizens, and could not be employed at managing positions. They recognised only one party, that is the SDS, as the ruling party, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you said it had a direct affect on members of your family. Are you aware of other people would be affected by this decision?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. My daughter, for example, that is my son-in-law, eventually lost his job because he did not respond to the call-up papers; That is, the order to report to the military unit. Furthermore, all of our colleagues who were on the list as delegates to the Municipal Assembly suffered various forms of harassment, including searches, and I heard people say that whenever such searches were carried out, they would be told that the best thing for them was to leave Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, before you move on. Mr. Smailagic, could you give the Trial Chamber information as to which newspaper this photocopy comes from? The name of the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was published in a local Banja Luka paper called Srpski Glas where I was able to read this. I'm not sure whether the same text was published in any other paper, but I personally read this in Srpski Glas magazine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And does the word "Srpski" -- the word "Glas," I know what it is, and the word "Srpski," I know what it is, but does the word "Srpski" indicate that this is a newspaper published by a particular party or a particular ethnic group in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It had already been taken over by the Party of Democratic Action. It concerned all -- all types of media, even the television was called the Serb television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. But what I mean to say, what -- was it a newspaper that belonged to one of the political parties existing in the area at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The paper was published by the Party of Democratic Action -- sorry, that is the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You will hear evidence about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, because the document itself does not state which newspaper it was taken from. So I had to know that. And also it is important to know whether the -- there is a political affiliation between this newspaper and some political party.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yeah, I agree, Your Honour. Before the adjournment, the witness mentioned that he read this particular article in Glas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but Glas, we have been hearing about Glas for the past three weeks and it seems to me that there was more than one Glas.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I agree. I agree. And we will hear more evidence so I won't -- I don't want to develop this subject right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, please proceed with the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Before, when we finish this Glas article, you were saying that people were encouraged to leave Banja Luka. Were people leaving Banja Luka in the period from April, 1992, until the end of the year?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were. There was a mass departure that occurred in May, I don't recall the exact date, when transport was organised with military vehicles and aircraft. Everybody had to leave under pressure. People were first taken to Belgrade and then from Belgrade via Hungary and other countries elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can I stop you? What was the nationality of that people who were leaving Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period of time, Bosniaks, Bosniaks were leaving Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you aware of any agencies or offices which would be set up in Banja Luka and which would help people leaving Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An agency had been established for immigration which was led by a lady called Perka whose surname I don't remember and Mr. Glogovac who had come to Banja Luka from Zenica. It was said that the agency had been established, that is, that the owner of the agency was Mr. Brdjanin, but there is no document to that effect. However, that was the rumour amongst the people. And finally the opinion prevailed. In order to leave --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Okay. Go on. You said in order to leave -- and I interrupted you. I will ask you again about these agencies. What was the purpose of these agencies? In which way did they help people to leave?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not actually help people. It helped the government at the time to ethnically cleanse the town of Banja Luka. Various transport companies were organised and they were very well paid. Whoever made a request to this agency for departure had to pay a hundred German marks per person which was a considerable sum of money at the time. One could live off 100 German marks for about a month in Banja Luka. That is for 30 marks, you could live for a month. In order to be given permission to leave, one had to have various kinds of papers, from the bank to the effect that they didn't have any debts, from the PTT organisation, from the power distribution company, from the water distribution company. They had to prove that they had settled all the costs and all the expenses that they had. And finally, they had to sign a statement whereby they were relinquishing their property to the municipality, the Serb municipality, that is, the municipality of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: To summarise what was the purpose of these agencies, it means that these agencies just organised the transportation of the people from Banja Luka elsewhere; is it correct it say?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you another question. Are you aware of vehicle who was generally called as a red Kombi in Banja Luka, at the time as we discussed before?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was common knowledge amongst the citizens of Banja Luka. All non-Serb citizens were afraid of this red Kombi, which would simply pick up people on the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you said that red Kombi would pick up, I don't think that the car itself would pick up. What did this red Kombi really mean?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Police officers were there. That is the driver and four or five police officers who were in this Kombi, and they would arrest people but some never returned. Some did return alive. Some returned injured and beaten up, but there were cases of people whose bodies were eventually found in the outskirts of Banja Luka. I know a person, that is, a family, where a son disappeared after he'd been arrested by the people in this red Kombi.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were they members of regular police?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you personally was ever picked by these members of red Kombi or by these police?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I want to move again and I want to ask you questions about Crisis Staff in Banja Luka. Was there Crisis Staff in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were two Crisis Staffs in Banja Luka. One was the Crisis Staff of the Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina and the other one was the Crisis Staff of the Banja Luka municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How did you learn about establishment of these Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The news were reported in the media, as far as I can remember. We knew who the leaders were and what the composition of these Crisis Staffs was, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you know the purpose of the Crisis Staff, of establishment of Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the war that had been declared by the Crisis Staff, that is the war situation, the state of war, it is my opinion that the purpose was to cleanse Banja Luka, not only Banja Luka but other regions as well of non-Serb population and they did it successfully.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When was Crisis Staff set up, or when you start knowing or when you were aware about the establishment, which period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992. I think that the Crisis Staffs were established sometime in May, mid-May or late May, after the outbreak of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you make distinguish and say who were members of each of these Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess I would object because this is clearly not the best evidence. There are documents that show who the members of these Crisis Staffs were, and his opinion of who they might have been is very far from the best evidence regarding this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not the best evidence, but it will give us, information as to how much the witness knows about the composition of these and whether he is on confusing, for example, some members in the municipality Crisis Staff with the other Crisis Staff for the Autonomous Region of Krajina. So the question is perfectly in order and I will allow it. Let's start with the Crisis Staff for the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Are you in a position to tell the Trial Chamber who were the members of that particular Crisis Staff? Is this okay with you, Ms. Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then we will move to the next one. Do you know who the members of the Crisis Staff of the ARK, of the Autonomous Region of Krajina were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Members of this regional staff were the head of the staff, that is Mr. Brdjanin; and a number of high-ranking officials of the SDS from Banja Luka, and neighbouring towns. For example, Mr. Vojo Kupresanin was one of the members. Stojan Zupljanin, and a number of others whose names I cannot recall at the moment. As for the municipal staff, the composition was different, but they acted in concert, because both Crisis Staffs had their seats in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you, by any chance, know who were the members of the municipal Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the municipal Crisis Staff, its president, by virtue of his office, was the head of the Banja Luka municipality, Mr. Predrag Radic. Andjelko Grahovac, Dr. Vukic, I believe, were also the members. Kasagic. And almost all of the members of the leadership, the municipal leadership of the SDS were also at the same time members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you follow decisions issued by Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Excuse me, did you follow decisions made by autonomous region Crisis Staff of Krajina, ARK?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The decision that we discussed a moment ago was one of the first decisions that were passed. It concerned employment, but there were others that I cannot remember at the moment. I cannot remember their topic. Mostly they concerned failure to respond to call-up papers, work obligation, restrictions on movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How did you learn about the content of these decisions? Were they published publicly?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were made public, that is, they were published. A couple of decisions were published by Srpski Glas, for example. But they were commented upon and broadcast over the Serb TV and radio, that is the Banja Luka TV and radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, I would like to summarise. You said that there were all kinds of restriction in life of non-Serb people in Banja Luka. Did you speak to anyone in authority about the wrongdoings and if they would be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. able to help improve the life of non-Serbs?
