utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one or two occasions, I had the opportunity of visiting the mayor at the time he was the president of the municipality in the Crisis Staff, Mr. Radic, with Mr. Safet Filipovic. So we considered that Radic had been a long-term citizen of Banja Luka. Before the war, he was a very eminent and respected man. He was communicative and it was possible to talk to him. We visited him but he made promises to us. He said that something -- that things would improve, but this all came to nothing. He made this promises but there were no results. And on one occasion, since he and Mr. Safet Filipovic were personal friends and were friends before the war, too, he said somewhere towards the end of the conversation, on the second visit, "It's best for to you collect your things and to leave. You can see what's happening here." That was, I mean, the end of everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Why didn't you complain to Mr. Brdjanin as president of the Crisis Staff, ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't have the courage in general terms. I'm not referring to security. And after all the statements he had made about us, to go and talk to him seemed to be quite futile. And also, we didn't want to skip levels. The municipal level, and go to him directly, because he could have helped us quite a lot. But this all came to nothing because this municipal level was under the regional level, after all, the Regional Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And now I would like to move to another topic again. You said -- you told us about all these restrictions. Did you try to inform the outside world about the life of non-Serb population in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did that very often. I think that we were lucky in that certain international organisations were in Banja Luka, among others, there was the International Red Cross, and we were -- we had very frequent contact with them and we presented all our problems to them. We also informed our government, the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was still a legal one, and in Sarajevo, and we informed our mission, the BH mission, to the United Nations, in order to inform the world of the situation in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What kind of information did you send to these organisations?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We informed them about the forcible -- about forcing people to carry out work obligations. People were taken to the front lines where the conflict was raging and they were made to dig trenches. They had to carry out -- people who were unfit for work were made to carry out work obligations. Age wasn't taken into account. People were simply gathered and taken off to work. We also informed about the general situation, about expulsions. At the time there was a lot of looting in Banja Luka. And I think that sometime in May or June, a lot of pressure was exerted on Banja Luka intellectuals of non-Serb nationality to leave Banja Luka -- in order to -- a well-known Banja Luka lawyer, Safeta Ibrisagic was found strangled in her flat with a so-called police wire and nothing was taken away, nothing was stolen. She was simply killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said at the beginning that "we" informed. Who were the people who participated in this handing over of information, of sending information?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We personally, from the Party of Democratic Action, we provided the information to our people. And as far as conversations with the International Red Cross is concerned, the UNHCR, we sometimes went with representatives of the Croatian government and with representatives of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You probably didn't understand what I meant. I meant when you say "we," who was it? It was you and who else?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Safet Filipovic, Mr. Muharem Krzic, Amir Novalija.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think that's enough. I don't want to develop this part because we have already heard evidence about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, she asked the question and I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he has answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He hasn't. She stopped him in the middle of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you know of any other persons, Mr. Smailagic, who participated in this continuous transmission of information to the various persons and organisations that you mentioned earlier, that is your government, the permanent mission in New York, International Red Cross and so on? You mentioned Mr. Krzic, you mentioned Mr. Filipovic, you mentioned Amir someone else, I can't remember the name. Was there anyone else who participated in this exercise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Asimir Krlic, Smail Djuzel, Asim Jakirlic, Mirsad Mehanovic. And then towards the end of 1992, they had already left Banja Luka, but before that, there was Ganic Bahut.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want him to go on, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please go on. Any other names that you can remember, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pribac but I can't remember his name right now. Sometimes Mr. Mehmet Krupic. And on one occasion, I have just remembered this, the Banja Luka mufti, Mr. Mahmut Ganic went to have conversations with the International Red Cross, was Mr. Halilovic. He was present at these talks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were there taken any actions against you and other people who were sending this information?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Among other things, I should first of all mention that during that period, from 1992 up until 1994, my house was searched on two occasions, but whenever it was searched, they said that they suspected that there were arms in my house, but on this occasion, when they searched my house, no arms were found. There was nothing there. Up until 1994, the 31st of August, when I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can I show the witness a document which was premarked as P464? It is in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you assist the judges and tell them what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- sorry, this is an indictment which was raised against -- issued against me and the people mentioned in the indictment, by the military court, the military Prosecutor's Office in Banja Luka and the security service centre in Banja Luka. We were accused of being involved in espionage. We were accused of being spies. On the basis of this indictment, we were arrested on the 31st of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you said you were accused of espionage, which period was covered by this indictment?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was from 1993, that's the year that they gave. I can't remember exactly. I can't read this right now. And most of the documents that they presented to the Court was composed of these reports that we had sent to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to the United Nations and to other international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can I show you another document which was premarked P465? This was the Registry. Tell us what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a sentence, a judgement, which was passed at the military court in Banja Luka in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were in the trial for the espionage based on the indictment which we previously saw. Did you have a lawyer at that time -- sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was offered to have a lawyer. I said I didn't have finance and that I couldn't have a lawyer. And then I was assigned by the judge someone called Zoran Opacic. At our first meeting with the investigating judge, the judge presented him as my assigned counsel. We met. The meeting was short. And I was then returned to my cell. However, at the second time I appeared before the investigating judge, in the presence of the lawyer Opacic he said, "I won't defend you. I've been to your house. I've asked your -- I asked your wife to pay me 5.000 marks. She didn't have such funds." And he said, "I won't work for free." I was then returned and after the indictment, I was informed at the court, by the president of the Chamber, that another lawyer had been assigned to me. Her name was Milika Maglov, a lawyer from Banja Luka, who was to defend me. Mrs. Maglov never came to the prison and not even to the Court in order to meet me, to talk to me about whether she could defend me. During the entire trial, she was silent, she remained silent, until the end of the trial, and when the defence had a closing argument to make. At that time, when she was supposed to make a statement, she only said one thing. "I leave it to the chamber to rule." That was what her Defence amounted to. And later, we the accused, were asked to make a statement. They -- the others had lawyers. I don't think that I and, Jakirlic didn't have lawyers. We had assigned counsel. When it was my turn to make a statement, I don't know why, maybe I was just feeling bad, I said, "I accept the Defence of my counsel." And even the Presiding Judge laughed at this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, before you proceed. Mr. Smailagic, you mentioned the name Milika Maglov. Do you see this person in this courtroom by any chance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the lady down there. She reminds me perhaps of her. I can now see that it's her. I think it is. If I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. We will talk about this later.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you convicted based on the indictment after the trial?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was sentenced to 11 years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the prison?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent 17 months in total in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to return, because you were indicted and convicted for espionage, and part of this conviction was that you were collected military-related information and trying to obtain weapons. Was it the case?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. And especially as far as weapons are concerned. We -- when we came into contact with the Bosniak people, we even tried to calm the situation, to make sure that no excesses occurred, since given that we knew about Banja Luka and its geographic position. We knew that it would not make any sense to try to mount a defence because it would all end tragically for everyone concerned. That was one of the reasons. And the other reason is the former JNA, Yugoslav People's Army, at the end of the war in Croatia, the all these forces were concentrated in Banja Luka. Therefore, it would not have made any sense to do something, to try and organise some kind of resistance. We always believed that the international community would have the possibility of bringing what was happening to an end and to improve the situation eventually. I'm not claiming that we didn't send information, but they considered the information we have mentioned -- they considered that the information that a citizen had lost his life, died, while carrying out his work obligation, or that a person called Nervin Nesovic when he was being taken away by the red Kombi, he was killed and thrown out in the street. I don't consider this to be espionage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No. My question was whether you collected military-related information.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't collect any kind of information, but what we found out from people we knew, friends, we would forward it because we thought that the state was the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that this was an attack against the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that it was our duty to the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina to report on all the changes, to report this to certain authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina and to report this to the international community. We sent the same information to the government in -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo, and we sent the same information to the mission, to the BH mission in the United Nations, and to the International Red Cross. There was information about killings, and let's say they -- they would try to conceal the casualties, the people who were killed. This had to be known. The world had to know about this, that they would take people to the Novo Groblje the new cemetery in Banja Luka. They would take them there in refrigerated lorries. They would do this every evening. Unfortunately, these were young people and they didn't know why they were dying.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you said they would take people to Novo Groblje, who were these people?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were soldiers, so-called soldiers in the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I close my appearance, I would like to show you a last document which was premarked P466. And if you could assist the Judges and tell us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the decision on cancelling the criminal proceedings against us who were accused. This decision was suspended. I'd like to say that I saw this decision in 1997, not before this. I didn't have the opportunity of receiving it. I didn't receive it personally. It was not until 1997 that I got it through Mrs. Filipovic, who was defending her brother, Safet Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Ms. Richterova. Have you discussed amongst yourselves, Mr. Ackerman and Maitre de Roux, who is going to start first?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would start first with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you want to pick up the matter that just came up in the examination regarding Ms. Maglov at this point or do you want to defer that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I think we can defer that. We don't need to discuss it in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that. Can I have just a moment to get prepared, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may go ahead, Mr. Ackerman, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Smailagic.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At the beginning of my questions to you, Mr. Smailagic, I will be referring to a large extent to two statements that you have given to the Office of the Prosecutor. You have given two statements to the Prosecutor's Office, have you not?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And one of those was a statement that you gave them in -- on 15 April of the year 2000 which we will refer to as statement number one, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And the second one was a statement that you gave on the 4th of June, the 14th of June, and the 19th of August, 2001, which we will refer to as statement number two, okay? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot confirm the dates. I know that I did give a statement but I'm no longer sure about the dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the Prosecutor to provide you with copies of the statement so you can look at them because I don't want to ask you questions about something that you can't look at. I want to be fair with you about these questions so let me ask the Prosecutor to provide him with his statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, let's establish first whether the witness can read English, read and understand English. Can you, Mr. Smailagic? Because I would imagine or rather I'm pretty sure that these statements are in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have them in B/C/S also, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have them in B/C/S also?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: They have been translated and we have the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, I would like confirmation from the witness himself whether he can read and understand English, the English language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you might as well give him the texts that you have in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you want to us show him also the B/C/S -- the English which was signed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Yes, please. Especially because I understand that it's only the English version that is signed by the witness, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And I would start with that. Mr. Smailagic, you have four documents there. Two are in the English language, two are in Serbo-Croat. I would like you to look at the two documents which are not in your language but which are in English, and I would like to know from you whether you can distinguish, whether you can see, on those documents, your signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, you will -- you are going to be asked questions with reference to those two statements and you will be allowed to refer to those statements before you give us your answer. Mr. Ackerman, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, we were talking about statement number two, and if you'll look at your B/C/S version of the statement, it's the one that has dates on it of 4 and 14 June and 19 August, 2001. Tell me if you see those dates. They would be on the face page, not the one you're looking at. It would not be the page you're looking at but -- there. About two-thirds of the way down that page, you should see the date of the interview and then you should see the dates that that interview occurred. Okay. And so you can confirm for me that there was -- there were three days, the 4th and 14th of June and the 19th of August of 2001, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Okay. You need to answer me audibly so that the translators can translate your answer instead of just nodding at me, and they'd appreciate that and I'd appreciate that because your answer needs to go into the record. Why did it take three days for this second statement to be prepared?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. All I know was that on several occasions, during these interviews, I asked for a break from the investigator because I was not feeling very well, and a moment ago, I just wanted to ask the Presiding Judge for a short break a 15-minute break if possible because I'm real any not feeling very well. My health is not at the best. So that was perhaps one of the reasons why this statement was taken over a period of time. That is with interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Are you saying now that you want to ask the Judge for a short break?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my intention, yes, in order to -- because after a while --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem with that. We will break for as long as is necessary. I will give it 20 minutes for the time being. If you need more, we will give you more. And I will give instructions that if either you need medical attention or if you need some coffee or some tea, you will be provided with that, or water or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just mention, because it's the second time it's come up, if Mr. Ackerman wants to know about why sometimes these statements are spread over days, I can call the investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have been given an explanation already.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because the same question was made to previous witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the explanation was that actually confirmation of information given and reconfirmation and also that other witnesses or other persons would be interviewed in the meantime on the same days. I think that is perfectly understood, but I would allow the question just the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. All I'm going to say if anything turns on it, in each case the investigators have notes as to why there are breaks or whatever and they are the persons to deal with it if anything turns on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. We will break for 20 minutes and please do attend to the witness and see what his needs are, and if we need to have a longer break, we will have a longer break. And if he needs anything, please make sure that he gets it. Okay? Thank you. We will break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. --- Break taken at 12.05 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Before we admit the witness again in the courtroom, Mr. Ackerman, while in chambers we were discussing amongst ourselves -- no, no, no. Before, I said. Please wait outside for a while. Thank you. We will in due course discuss what emerged this morning, namely that your co-counsel was defence -- was counsel for the witness in the espionage proceedings of 1994. Irrespective of what may or may not have implied, irrespective of whether there should be any decision taken in regard, I think, and we are in agreement in this, that for the time being, while the witness is giving evidence, especially now that he is being cross-examined by your team, of which Ms. Maglov forms part, we are going to suggest to you to agree that while this is taking place, Ms. Maglov will absent herself from the courtroom. It will help the witness to feel more at ease and it will pave the way for a more reasonable approach, a practical, pragmatic approach to the problem when we come to it, when and if we need to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept that. It's -- this is a matter of course that is somewhat troubling. I first became aware of the problem fairly recently, where I come from it would be an absolute bar to her appearing as counsel in this case. I've been informed that that is not the rule in this Tribunal, that in at least one case, a lawyer who the Prosecution thought they might want to use as a witness, because his name was all over documents in the case, was allowed to continue representing a defendant in the case. So what I would have thought, had this occurred in the United States, may not be the case here, but I do recognise the issue very clearly, and with that in mind, I have not asked Ms. Maglov to share with me any information that she may have obtained from this witness in the course of a confidential attorney-client relationship, because that would make it highly improper. And so I have scrupulously avoided asking her those kinds of questions and will continue to do so. I think -- I don't know what the position of the Prosecutor is with regard to this. I think that may be important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think for the time being, leave the Prosecution alone. We are dealing directly with you as a Trial Chamber for the time being. We are not discussing the issue as such. We just made a proposition to you, a suggestion, and I am using the words, the nouns, proposition and suggestion, to indicate that this is a direct approach that we are taking with you as lead counsel in this case. We still have to discuss it amongst ourselves in any case, because as you can imagine, we did not have as much time. We know about the other case that you mentioned because in the meantime, we have obviously asked for information. And also basing ourselves on what happened in the previous -- in the other case, it's also basing ourselves on what happened in the other case that we are making this proposition to you. And I think it will make things easier. I don't think I need to explain further for the time being. I think you are understanding me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I accept the suggestion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also appreciate your loyalty to the Trial Chamber and also to the Prosecution in affirming that you have specifically avoided asking questions or seeking information from Ms. Maglov in regard to what may or may not have taken place in 1994 when she represented Mr. Smailagic. The Trial Chamber wishes to put that on record. You have been -- you have showed a lot of loyalty so far and that is appreciated by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I better make the record clear. I have talked with her about the allegation that she was his counsel. I have not asked her anything about any private, protected, attorney-client communication she had with him because that's where I think the impropriety would exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We definitely would have appreciated this information to have come forward from you or Ms. Maglov directly at the beginning of the evidence of Mr. Smailagic because I think it would have spared us all this maybe unnecessary waste of time but any way, I take it that Ms. Maglov accepts to absent herself from the courtroom while Mr. Smailagic continues with his -- continues being cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Maglov. Mr. Brdjanin, in case this has been beyond your understanding, I am sure that Mr. Ackerman will explain this to you at some point in time, later on, because I don't want you to go back with the idea that this Trial Chamber has capriciously deprived you for an hour or two from one of the lawyers representing you. There is a reason for doing this and for the time being. Then there will be a full opportunity to have this discussed and to listen, to hear the views which Mr. Ackerman, representing you, may have on the matter and also what the Prosecution may have on the matter. But there may be a case of possible conflict of interest, which -- or also possible ethical conduct which we may have to go into. We need to study it further and of course, your lead counsel will have ample opportunity to inform -- to give his reasons to the Trial Chamber. I wanted you to know that there is a reason why we had to make the suggestion to your lead counsel for the time being. Have you understood me? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] I fully understand the reasons, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Brdjanin. Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can just remind Your Honours and Mr. Ackerman that I would be grateful if we could have ten minutes at the end of the session. Mr. Smailagic will obviously be still here tomorrow where I can just deal with the Stakic matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So bring in Mr. Smailagic, please. Yes, Mr. Smailagic, are you feeling better now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ackerman, representing Mr. Brdjanin, will be resuming his cross-examination of you. If at any time you feel uncomfortable and you need further -- a further break, please do not hesitate to let the Trial Chamber know that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, if you find yourself not feeling well again, please feel free to advise us, okay? I have an additional question to ask you with regard to both of these statements. There came a time, did there not, starting with the first one, when an actual written statement was presented to you and you were asked to sign the statement. That would be the English version of number one, the 15 April version. You in fact signed that. The Judge has already confirmed that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And before you signed it, you were given an opportunity to be completely familiar with the contents of the statement, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And so when you signed it, you knew what you were signing?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And the same would be true of the second statement, which I presume you signed on 19 August, 2001, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Since you have come to The Hague or prior to your coming to The Hague, have you had a chance to review both of your statements?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When was the last time you had a chance to review your statements?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement was read back to me after it had been taken from me, from -- by the investigator in Zenica and with the assistance of the interpreter, I accepted it as such and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you have not seen it since then?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. At least not in the translation into Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, could you please ask the witness whether he was given a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's where I'm going.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you give and copy of your statement in the translation, in the B/C/S version, ever?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think that makes it very difficult for me to ask him about his statements since he's never been provided with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it may be if it's put more directly, when he came here on the weekend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You gave it to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- he was given a statement. It wasn't dealt with by me, but I think that may get the answer required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I suggest to you, Mr. Ackerman to put a direct question to him to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, since you have come to The Hague, has anyone handed you a copy of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I believe it was on Saturday, and I had an opportunity to read it at that time, in Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And so you have read both of your statements recently?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did anyone interfere with your reading? Did you have complete freedom to read them at your leisure, for as long as you wanted?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Tell me, as you sit here today, if all of the statements that you made, in each of those statements, was a true statement.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I made a correction, an error may have occurred in interpretation on two occasions, I believe. In the first statement, there is a mistake. There is maybe a mistake in the second one as well but I cannot find it. On page 146, in the first statement, you could read the words "Brdjanin's wife, Perka." I was maybe referring to her as a woman not as a wife actually. It's the way we speak. And that is the reason why I said that he -- she probably was not his wife. I just meant a woman that he worked with. So that was one correction. And then another one, where mention was made of the young man who was killed, Nerko Mesinovic and then Smail Djuzel is the name that follows immediately after that. It was not from Smail Djuzel or his father that I heard that. I heard the information from the father of Nerko Mesinovic. It was from the father that I heard that he had been taken in this car. So these would have been my remarks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And back when you originally signed these statements you didn't notice these mistakes?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't -- I wasn't paying attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So when you signed the statements, swearing that they were true, you weren't paying attention?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are probably correct. That was probably the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It's the case, isn't it, and I suggest to you that it's the case, that when the investigators came to speak to you the second time, after your first statement in which you had made certain allegations, when the investigators came to speak with you the second time in June of 2001, the investigators told you that some of the things you said in your first statement were not true and that you needed to correct them. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were some instances that I got mixed up. I was confused. You must understand the kind of situation I was in, both physically and psychologically. Sometimes I even today I feel that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you being put under any kind of pressure by the investigators from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In your first statement, the one of 15 April, 2000, I'll ask you to look at the second paragraph of that statement. In that paragraph, you mention that although the 1991 census showed there were 28.000 Muslims living in Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Registered. Not living, registered.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. Registered in Banja Luka, there were actually 52.000 Muslims living there,. That's what you said, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I stand by that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And that would have been, in your view, the number living there in 1991, when the census was taken?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what do you think the number was in 1992, in April of 1992? Would it have been roughly the same number?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been some slight changes because people had already started leaving. I said that, in May, a military transport was organised to take people out of Banja Luka. Do you want me to explain the difference between the census and the actual number that I mentioned, that is 52.000, 52.300 or so Muslims living in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I take it it's your position that those people who in the census called themselves Yugoslavs were predominantly Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think you would also agree, wouldn't you, that a significant Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. number of people who called themselves Yugoslav would have been Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And wouldn't it be fairer to say that this figure that you've come up with of 52.000 represented both Muslims and Croats, in other words non-Serbs, living in the Banja Luka municipality and not just Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This figure, 52.000, represents only Muslims, and I can clarify, if you want me to, my reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will ask you to tell me on what basis you made the determination that the vast majority of those people who designated themselves as Yugoslavs were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should like the Presiding Judge to allow me to explain this in somewhat greater detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, start explaining it, and then we'll see how much further detail you will be allowed to give. But try to be as concise as possible. I mean there should be a very simple explanation. Probably it's historical. And you obviously are showing us that you know something about it or you are giving us that indication, but try to be as short as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best, Your Honour. I'll try to be as brief and as clear as possible. I have already told you about the referendum that was organised in Banja Luka in February or March, 1992. In order for such a referendum to be held, it was necessary to compile lists with voters. The lists are kept at the Banja Luka municipality. And as we were carrying out preparations for this referendum, we asked the Banja Luka municipality to provide us with electoral lists on the basis of which the referendum could be organised. We also asked for the stamps of the electoral commissions, which we did on two occasions. But on both of these occasions, we were refused. After that, we went to the state Ministry of Administration in Sarajevo, where we were given electoral lists, including the lists of all citizens of Banja Luka, by names and surnames. And it was on the basis of that that we were able to have the number of all citizens in Banja Luka who were allowed to vote. This number here, 52.000, does not include children. So the document in question was a reliable document, issued by state authorities, which existed at the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it was there that we were given the stamps for electoral commissions so that the referendum could be held, which was indeed carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have given us a lot of information, but you have not answered the question that was put to you by Mr. Ackerman. Please look at the second paragraph of your first statement. And there you have two affirmations. The first affirmation is that according to the findings following the census in 1991, there were 28.000 persons registered in Banja Luka who are described now here by you as Muslims. Now, this is a census, and as I understand it, if I am wrong please correct me, a census has got absolutely nothing to do with a referendum, or what is commonly referred to as the electoral list of voters. Then you move forward and make an assertion, if not an affirmation, that in fact, however, although the census result showed 28.000 Muslims registered in Banja Luka, there were 52.000 Muslims living there. There is a discrepancy of 22.000 individuals here. What Mr. Ackerman wants to know from you is on what basis, what knowledge do you have on the basis of which you found it yourself comfortable in making this affirmation. In other words, how can we be assured that although there were 28.000 Muslims registered in Banja Luka, according to the census, in reality, there were 52.000 Muslims? How can we know that you know what you're talking about? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me try to explain. The statistics were given to us on the basis of lists of citizens. The source of which was the Ministry of the Interior. The lists included the names and surnames of all residents there and it was possible to establish the number of 52.000 or so Muslims. However, as for the census in 1991, people declared themselves as Serbs, Muslims, Croats and there was another category which was titled "undeclared." I don't know what happened later on with this category in Slovenia and Croatia, for example. But it was on the basis of that category that some people declared themselves as Yugoslavs, but I must tell you something else. This former Yugoslavia was actually the best solution for us in -- I mean, in the old times, and that was the reason why people declared themselves as Yugoslavs and most of such cases are from the regions that are predominantly Muslims and that is the reasons why you have figures and statistics as such in this census, that is that there was a certain number of Muslims, Croats, Serbs Yugoslavs and others. As for the lists from the Ministry of the Interior, we had precise information, that is we had all names and surnames of the citizens living there and it was on the basis of that list that I was able to assert that there were 52.000 or maybe 52.250 Muslims living in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think, Mr,. Ackerman that answers your question or mine, whichever way you prefer to put it and you can proceed with the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So I take it you actually sat with those voting lists and counted the number of people who had names that you could recognise as Muslim names and you came up with 24.000 that you counted off those lists. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not only names but also surnames and not only 24.000 but 52.000 in total.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you looked at those lists and counted 52.000 people that you concluded were Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long did that take you?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible to establish that very fast. The lists were obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: My question, though, was how long did that take you to count 52.000 people from those lists?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have to count them. They were numbered. Their names were listed under numbers. We got the list with specific names and surnames.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you had a stack of paper with names and surnames, numbered from 1 through 52.000?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there is maybe a misunderstanding. The lists were broken down according to local communes, and we knew immediately the figures for a particular local commune. We didn't have to, for example, consult the list for the Stricic local municipality where only certificate Serbs lived or Debeljaci where only Croats lived or the local commune of Ivanjska also populated exclusively by Croats. Muslims lived mostly in the town. There was only one Muslim, exclusively Muslim village in the vicinity of Banja Luka, Bastasi, where 90 to 100 Muslim families lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: But there were a lot of mixed areas, too, that had Muslims, Croats and Serbs living in them, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you had to go through those lists and make a separation and count how many of those were in fact Muslim, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I go back it my question. How long did this process take you?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, the whole procedure at that time, we weren't interested in this. When the referendum was held. We were interested in all citizens as far as the referendum is concerned. And then later, when they started abusing figures and the commitment of people, whether they had declared themselves to be Slovene or Muslim, at that point we presented all the information. Whether it took five days or two weeks or a month it's impossible for me to say now. But then we could see that it was necessary for the real situation to be discovered, and to report on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you say "we" there were other people helping you do this counting, then, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me clarify this. I didn't -- I didn't conduct this numbering. I only assisted to the extent that I was able to, and when I was able to. Naturally, there was several people, there were a number of people who were involved in this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If it has been established earlier in this trial that the population of Banja Luka municipality was 48.4 per cent Serb, 14.8 per cent Croat, and 14.6 per cent Muslim, would you agree or disagree with those figures?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You wouldn't what?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With those numbers, I would, if we are talking about how people declared themselves, that they declared themselves to be Muslims or Croats or Serbs and Yugoslavs. And the category of others, which is a category which existed with us. But if we are talking about the numbers of Muslims, then I can't accept that figure of 14 per cent. But only the other one that I mentioned earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So if someone testified here that the number of Muslims was 14.6 per cent, they were in error?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't an error because he took the information from the statistics of the -- from the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I want to move forward. I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours I have an exhibit, DB 42A. This is a document that was supplied to us by the OTP and no -- I don't think there was a B/C/S translation ever done of the document, at least if there is, I don't have it. But I think we need to put it on the ELMO. If there is a B/C/S translation, it would be helpful to have it, but I don't think there is one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, this is going to be a little bit difficult because we only have this in the English language, and so I will simply tell you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are just checking. There may be a translation but we are just checking.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will simply tell you that what this is is an article from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you wait a minute, Mr. Ackerman, until we verify whether there is a translation because that would simplify matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: There is a B/C/S translation of this document which was disclosed to the Defence. However, we don't have it right now with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have a suspicion that this document was filed with the first batch. What number -- what number does it show on your records?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, are you referring to ERN number, this M000 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. It's -- I have seen this before, or at least there was a reference to it before, Roy Gutman, or at least he was mentioned by Mr. Krzic as one of the persons that he was -- that he contacted, and the name appears in one of the reports submitted to the secret service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's absolutely right. Mr. Krzic was asked about meetings with Mr. Gutman but this article in itself was not being produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But we can -- if Mr. Ackerman can wait until tomorrow for this, we believe he has a copy but we can find a copy ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, during my cross-examination of Mr. Krzic, I put it on the ELMO and referred him to one paragraph of it but I don't think I ever marked it or had it admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, you didn't, in fact, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I again only want to refer to one paragraph, very short, and I think I could just read it to him and ask him if he accepts it. If the Prosecutor wants to give him a B/C/S copy and ask him further questions about this document, they are certainly free to do so. I will do what Your Honour suggests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can -- no, no. We can move ahead along those lines. Mr. Smailagic, we have a document here which unfortunately, for the time being, is only in English. You're not going to be asked questions on the entire document, but only on a very short paragraph which counsel, Mr. Ackerman, is going to read out in English, and while he is reading it out, it will be translated into your own language by the interpreters. So basically, the importance of having the document in your own language or in English, in the English language, does not arise more -- any more. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. President, the interpreters do not have a copy of this exhibit, and would need it in order to translate it. Do you have extra copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They have it. We gave it to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm seeing the Nero sign. Please proceed, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We try very hard to take good care of our interpreters, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm very sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Smailagic, this -- I'll tell you what this document is. It's an article from Newsday, which is a newspaper published on Long Island, in New York, United States of America. The article is written by a fellow by the name of Roy Gutman. I take it you have heard of Mr. Gutman.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. More or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Have you ever met Mr. Gutman?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Gutman met on at least one occasion with Muharem Krzic and was a recipient of information from Muharem Krzic?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muharem Krzic met several of these people. He met journalists and representatives of the international community and finally, as president of the Party of Democratic Action, he was authorised to have contact with them and to make statements, to issue statements for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I understand that. My only question was, do you know specifically if he met with Mr. Gutman?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember now. That was a long time ago, after all. I'm not sure. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Part of this article I want to read to you is very short, and my question will be: Do you accept what Mr. Gutman says? I'm going to read to you the fourth paragraph on the first page, where Mr. Gutman reports as follows: "At least 50.000 Muslims and Croats remain in Banja Luka, Bosnia's second biggest city and the capital of the breakaway Serb area." That's the statement. The date is 26 September, 1992. Do you agree or disagree with that number as reported by Mr. Gutman?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since he didn't say an exact number but provided an approximate number, I agree with that. I mentioned that from April or May, they started -- people started leaving Banja Luka, both Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You have -- you've said in your statement on page 2, that Mr. Brdjanin was a member of the executive board of the SDS in Banja Luka. Do you stand by that assertion?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You have said in your testimony here today, and in your statement, that Mr. Brdjanin attended SDS joint meetings, SDS-SDA in the Dom Kultura, in the fall of 1991, as a member of the SDS executive board of Banja Luka. Do you stand by that assertion?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On several occasions, he attended and in the course of the summer, I think that a while ago, I said that he was not only present at those meetings but I was there on a daily basis in our premises. We were very close to each other and I would see him there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I suggest to you that Mr. Brdjanin was never a member of the SDS executive board in Banja Luka, never a member of the SDS in Banja Luka, never attended a meeting of the SDS in Banja Luka, and never attended any meetings which you speak of in 1991. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a number of questions there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Ackerman, please go through the list again, and he will be asked to reply to each and every one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm trying to do this curious thing that the English call "putting it to the witness" which we never heard of it America, and I'll try to do it properly. I'm just struggling with this, Your Honour. And Ms. Korner has tried to explain it to me, but apparently not well enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Let me try to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The first one was that Mr. Brdjanin was a member of the executive board of the SDS in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I suggest to you that he was not a member of the executive board of the SDS in Banja Luka. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I suggest to you that he was not a member, ever, of the SDS in Banja Luka. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I suggest to you that he never attended a meeting of the SDS in Banja Luka. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I suggest to you that he never engaged in any meetings, joint Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. meetings, between SDA and SDS members in Banja Luka in the fall of 1991, as you have testified. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAHUDIN SMAILAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: On page 3 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, whenever it is convenient for you, remember, please, we have -- we need ten minutes on other matters. I don't want to interrupt you but if you can possibly conclude this particular part of your cross-examination between now and the next three minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm actually getting ready to start a new subject. This would be a good time to stop, and we probably need more than ten minutes anyhow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. So, Mr. Smailagic, we have to stop now because there are other matters that need to be debated in this courtroom. You will be returning to this courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00, when Mr. Ackerman will hopefully conclude his cross-examination, and then you will also be cross-examined by the Defence team for General Talic. I thank you for your patience. And you can withdraw. You may withdraw now and we will see you tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just before you leave -- okay. He won't understand me in English in any case. I just wanted to remind him not to have any contact at all with the next witness but I'm sure that they are not --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no problem with that. I think he's taken the warning to heart. Your Honour, before I deal with what was raised yesterday in the Stakic case, can I say that I think sooner rather than later Your Honours should hear exactly from an investigator how a statement is taken. I propose to put in as soon as this witness is finished shortly, Mr. Dupas, the investigator who took the statement, so that Your Honours can hear the method by which it's taken. Your Honour, can I now turn to what happened yesterday in the Stakic Status Conference, which has an effect on this trial? As Your Honours know, but the Defence in this case may not know, the same team for the Prosecution has conduct of the Stakic case. The Prosecution yesterday was ordered by Judge Schomburg to -- firstly, I'm sorry, I should say the trial of Stakic, depending on finance, apparently, is provisionally listed to start on the 17th of April. I'm sorry, the 16th of April. That has this effect that, by that stage, we shall have left Prijedor in this case because of the Stakic case, and be -- we anticipate, be engaged in the Sanski Most municipality evidence. Judge Schomburg then made an order that the Prosecution should file in the Stakic case and in this case separate motions for the witnesses in the Prijedor segment, which are common to this case and to Stakic, which I should say is effectively the same all bar, I believe we counted nine, seeking to depose those witnesses, to have evidence taken by way of deposition, and the suggestion made by Judge Schomburg was that each Trial Chamber would make its own ruling as to whether depositions were appropriate. And if each Trial Chamber came to the conclusion, having heard from the Defence on -- in both cases, that witnesses were suitable for deposition, then the idea was that the deposition will be conducted with a presiding officer, unspecified. There will be one examination-in-chief and then, if the witness is one that both cases or the Defence in both cases wish to cross-examine, then there will be cross-examination by effectively three different counsel. So Your Honour, that's the suggestion that was made. The Prosecution will accordingly file in each case a motion as to which witnesses should be the subject of depositions. One of the matters that was raised by Judge Schomburg was this: That it would be preferable that some depositions took place before the beginning of the Stakic trial. Now, Your Honour, that does seem to us on the Prosecution side to raise exceeding difficulties because we shall be sitting until the end of March, bar the one week. One suggestion was made that we should deal with this trial in the morning and then all counsel would be expected to deal with Prijedor witnesses in the afternoon in deposition form. I think that may cause considerable difficulty, perhaps less for us, because we can allocate members of our team separately but certainly for Defence counsel. I'm raising it at this stage, as I say, so that both the Defence counsel in this case know. Did I ask that a transcript of yesterday's proceedings should be provided to the Defence in this case and so that one can take cognizance of the fact of what's going to happen. Our concern is that if the Stakic provisional date is proceeded with, then there is no crossover with this trial. And I'm raising it before Your Honours. It will be Your Honours' decision as to how to deal with this but it would be preferable, we consider, that both Trial Chambers should be starting Prijedor at the same time, but I merely raise this, as I say, as a matter to inform Defence counsel. I have no doubt Your Honours will be informed by Judge Schomburg of his ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. I would imagine, from the looks of Mr. Ackerman and from the looks of Maitre de Roux, that this is all news to you and that obviously I would -- it would be very unfair on my part, on our part, to expect any sort of reaction from you for the time being. I understand, Ms. Korner, that you are going to file these motions?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We are going to file motions saying which witnesses -- effectively I think it will be the same. We are going to file the same motion but addressed to different Trial Chambers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously, composed differently, too. I happen to be in both for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ah, we were told it was going to be two ad litem judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's when there is said that the trial will start.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be the trial stage. For the time being we are in the Pre-Trial stage as far as that case is concerned, while we are in the trial stage as far as this is concerned. So that tends to complicate matters as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any way, we'll see. You will find me cooperative. However, you need to realise that we are talking of two different compositions for the time being. Yes, Mr. Ackerman, or Maitre de Roux, I mean you both stood up more or less at the same time. I don't know who to address first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let Mr. De Roux --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The in the meantime you get time too think about it more. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm a little surprised because we are here judging the accused, General Talic, within the scope of an indictment. And the hearing here and now, which is in this indictment, and what the objection that the Defence is making, the charge the Defence is making about this act, and suddenly we are being -- they are suggesting that we interrogate, examine witnesses, at the same time and in the light of another indictment, with which we are not acquainted. And obviously, this falsifies, this stocks the matter. We are not judging the Prijedor case. We are judging the General Talic case with evidence that the Prosecution considers to have gathered. And I think that if we abandon this logic, we will commence a new trial. We will be entering into a new trial. As far as I know, Mr. Stakic, the mayor of Prijedor, has never been examined with regard our indictment, and I don't think it is the time right now, it's a little late, to try by having recourse to common hearings. I don't think it is right to try and mix two indictments or otherwise in such a case, it would be very complicated. We would have to do a joinder. I think that the Prosecution will file a motion, we will respond to it, but I think this trial is too far advanced for us to abandon the indictment raised against General Talic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you Maitre de Roux. Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I respond to that before Mr. Ackerman? Your Honour, I don't think that Mr. De Roux appreciates the procedures. It's under Rule 71. It is not suggested that there is going to be a joinder. It is simply a method of not having to bring back the same witnesses to this Court twice. It doesn't mix the two cases as such, but the evidence is from -- examination-in-chief is identical in both cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I understand it, Ms. Korner, the whole idea is that one option, I must say an undesirable option, would be to introduce inside this trial while the witnesses are here, Mr. Stakic, who is under another indictment, with possibly two Trial Chambers, three different Defence teams, and that would be a confusion -- confusion, organised confusion. And would certainly not work. So what I understand, if I read you well, I still have to go through the minutes of the records of the transcript of yesterday's Status Conference, if I read you well, -- since that is not feasible, I mean practically, there is no way it can be done, there is a simpler way of doing it, by having these witnesses come here at a certain point in time before the Stakic case starts, and we will have absolutely nothing to do with the Stakic case. These witnesses will be questioned, examined and cross-examined, by the three different teams, not in open court as we are here, but in -- during a session which is -- which falls within in parameters of Rule 71, chaired by a --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Presiding officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, as presiding officers, as conceived in that section because he is conceived in a different way in another section, in another rule, and then with the understanding that since there will be a representation of the Defence in this case, and the Defence in the other case, that the evidence will be brought forward in this case, which is the one we are interested in, and it will be sort of taken as read because you would have conducted your examination-in-chief and they would have conducted their cross-examination. This is how I understand it, if I am reading you well because I may be confusing the issue in my mind as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour is absolutely right. That's what is intended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Ackerman, please may I -- I have been give and note here that we must end now. And they need time to prepare for Simic so if you could keep your brief -- well, obviously we are not deciding anything on this. I still have to read the transcript and give you all the opportunity to come back to the Trial Chamber on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me have 20 seconds, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even more, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All I want to say right now is this, and I'll have a lot more to say later. This problem was created by the Prosecution by multiply indicting a number of people for the events that happened in this area and now they are seeking help from the Defence in that -- and the Chamber to solve the problem that they have created. And I'm willing to help in that regard. And I think the Chamber is willing to help in that regard. But I'm not willing to sacrifice the fair trial that my defendant is entitled to and the rights that my defendant is entitled to just to help the Prosecution solve this problem. And we shouldn't do that. That's expediency taking over justice. And we can't let that happen. I do not want to get involved in taking depositions where counsel for Stakic are in the room examining the witness at the same time we are. Because that creates motivations to do things that are mischievous that couldn't possibly happen in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any way, I understand, Ms. Korner that you will be filing, the OTP will be filing the relative motions. And you will have ample opportunity, of course, to respond to them. And we will take the matter afterwards when the response -- the necessary responses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was simply to given the Defence warning because they suddenly got motions and they had no idea what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. I thank you all. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
